title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Construction-site clean-up
audience: Solo operators and team owners of construction-site clean-up businesses who want site work from principal contractors and builders in their service area.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, project size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a site clean-up need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. For site clean-up, write down the project sizes you can staff, the trades you can work alongside, the price range you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each principal contractor runs projects. A principal contractor with several projects in your area is worth more to a small business than a single project across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. If you cannot state them, you cannot tell a good lead from a poor one.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who makes the buying decision, and whether the work falls within the licence and insurance you hold. Principal contractors and builders are the likely buyers, because they control the site and its housekeeping. Add a prospect only when it passes the criteria. Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from. Write one short profile for each segment, as business.gov.au suggests when identifying a target market (24 September 2024), and test your assumptions with Victorian guidance on who buys (business.vic.gov.au, undated). Keep only business contact details published for business use, and do not buy or harvest contact lists. ACMA's guidance says buying a list does not remove the need to show consent (last updated 28 March 2019, an older source). Whether the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business depends on its turnover and other factors, so check the OAIC's guidance. Its coverage is not confirmed in the research file.

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a project is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely in the near future. For site clean-up, the useful signals are a planning permit for a project of a size you can serve, a building permit with an estimated cost, a public notice of works, and a public tender for a building project. Some councils publish planning permit registers with suburb, category and status fields, such as the City of Casey register, so check your own council's register (DataVic, last updated 5 November 2026). A register shows the stage of an application, not when work will start, so confirm timing with the principal contractor. The Victorian building permit dataset records each permit with its location, estimated cost and issue date (DataVic, last updated 28 August 2026). Use that data to see which suburbs have active projects, and remember the code's $250,000 threshold is a cost test under the 2015 construction code rather than a tool for picking prospects; confirm how the cost is measured in the instrument before you rely on it. In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists public tenders for public building work (last updated 7 August 2026). Federally, AusTender lists open tenders and publishes awarded contracts of $10,000 or more (Department of Finance, undated). The Commonwealth Cleaning Services Guidelines were revoked from 1 July 2014, so do not use them as current tender rules (PM&C, 2014).

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: Before you make an offer, confirm the scope, your capacity and the deadline (Business Queensland, last updated 16 November 2022). A useful first message does three things. It states how you came to know about the project or the notice. It makes one specific observation that you can verify from public view or from the principal contractor's own published material, such as a permit or a notice about works. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined stage or a fifteen-minute call. Send it to the principal contractor's office or tender team, not to site staff. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. ACMA says marketing messages need consent, and that consent should be recorded. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading. About 80 per cent of respondents said unsolicited selling seldom gave useful information or offers, and about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. A pattern to test is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, followed by a pause. The research does not source this interval, so treat it as a starting point. Where a principal contractor runs a formal tender or approval process, follow its rules rather than your schedule. Stopping is part of the approach. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. Every unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days (ACMA). At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

procedure: Write the project size, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the site work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, such as planning permits and building permits, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message and do-not-call rules and the licence rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit principal contractors first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A small site clean-up business covers three suburbs. A council planning permit for a project in one suburb shows an application status change, and the builder's business email address is published on the builder's website. The owner also notices that the builder's project manager's personal mobile number appears on a site board.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner send a sales message to the builder now, what should it contain, and should the personal mobile number be used?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner should not send a sales email just because the builder's address is published. ACMA's Spam Act obligations page says publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages (last updated 28 March 2019), and the research file warns not to assume a business-to-business exemption. The permit register shows the application stage, not when work will start, so the owner first checks whether the builder has agreed to receive messages or has invited contact. If neither applies, the owner waits for an invitation or uses a route the builder has agreed to. The personal mobile number on the site board is not used at all, because it was not published for business use. For a phone call to a business number, the owner checks the Do Not Call Register guide and calling-hour limits, and treats them as applying until checked. Any message that does go out names the project, says how the business learned of it, offers one specific stage it could clean, and asks one question. The owner does not enter the site without an invitation and follows the site rules.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, project size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules and induction

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to every principal contractor on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using a personal number seen on a site board, or private information about a worker, to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that you are not licensed or insured to deliver, or approaching site staff directly.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance the state where the work is done requires before outreach, and send first approaches to the principal contractor's office.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. This lesson does not grant any licence. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check the rule for each one you work in. Whether site clean-up is construction work, and which WHS rules then apply, is checked against the 2015 construction code and state rules, not settled by this lesson.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says the Act also covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. Marketing messages need consent, which should be recorded, and every unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days (ACMA, 'Avoid sending spam'). Phone calls to business numbers face the calling-hour limits described in the do-not-call guide (2018 copyright notice). The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing, a permit register or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, the OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7) says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Its coverage of small business is not confirmed in the research file. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen and the stage it showed.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the site work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, but remember a register shows stage, not start date. Never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off project well outside your service area, because it looks large
A principal contractor with several projects inside your service area that you already work near
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A council permit register shows a project near your service area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the principal contractor about the project, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each worker on the site using their personal contact details and ask them to sign up for the work
Go onto the site to look at the work before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must accurately identify the sender and include correct contact details for at least 30 days; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option that is free, works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. The page as read does not name the Spam Act 2003 and does not cover privacy law. Publisher: Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA).
